explanations.explanation: That's the opening line on Job: "blameless and upright, fearing God and shunning evil." The writer gives us his character before anything happens to him. I'd love an introduction like that. Mine would be "came out of a closing bakery with a price sticker on him."

Not a hint of that in verse 1. The Bible calls Job "blameless and upright." It also says he feared God and shunned evil, so he's a humble man, friend. Proud and stubborn would make a very different story.

The writer never calls Job clever or cunning. Verse 1 says he was "blameless and upright, fearing God and shunning evil." That's about his character, not about being sneaky or sharp. Job isn't running any schemes.

Yes, friend. Verse 3 says, "Job was the greatest man of all the people of the East." It comes right after the list of his flocks, herds and servants. That's a whole lot of cookie boxes' worth of stuff.

The text says the opposite. Job 1:3 says, "Job was the greatest man of all the people of the East." The verse just finished counting his sheep, camels, oxen, donkeys and servants. Nobody in the East outranked him.

He sends for his children to purify them. Then he rises early in the morning to offer burnt offerings for all of them. Nobody asks him to get up that early, and he does it anyway. I can barely get up early for a fresh batch.

explanations.answer: Gives each of them a flock
explanations.explanation: Job has plenty of sheep, but this verse isn't about handing out flocks. After the feasting he rises early to offer burnt offerings for all of them (Job 1:5). The text says nothing about flocks going to his children.

explanations.answer: Throws a feast of his own
explanations.explanation: The feasts belong to his sons, who take turns holding them in their homes (Job 1:4). When those days are over, Job has something else to do. He rises early and offers burnt offerings for all of his children.

explanations.answer: He thinks they may have sinned
explanations.explanation: The text gives us Job's own thought: "Perhaps my children have sinned and cursed God in their hearts." That's why he offers burnt offerings for all of them. I think that tells us how seriously Job takes his children's hearts. He doesn't wait to find out. He covers them in advance.

explanations.answer: A priest has told him to
explanations.explanation: No priest shows up in this passage. The reason the Bible gives is Job's own thought: "Perhaps my children have sinned and cursed God in their hearts." This is his idea. He's the one rising early.

explanations.answer: He made a vow to God
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't mention a vow anywhere. It tells us what Job thinks: "Perhaps my children have sinned and cursed God in their hearts." That thought is the reason the burnt offerings happen.
Not quite. Job didn't do this one time and call it done. Verse 5 ends with, "This was Job's regular practice." He did it when the days of feasting were over, every time around.

Right, it wasn't a one-time thing. Verse 5 says, "This was Job's regular practice." Each time the days of feasting were over, he rose early to offer burnt offerings for his children. That's a man who keeps showing up, friend.

That's what Satan says. The full answer is, "From roaming through the earth, and walking back and forth in it." The LORD asks where he's come from, and that's his answer. Short and plain, no extra details.
Egypt never comes up in this scene. Satan answers the LORD with, "From roaming through the earth, and walking back and forth in it." He names no country at all.
Nineveh isn't mentioned here, friend. When the LORD asks, Satan says, "From roaming through the earth, and walking back and forth in it." He doesn't name a single city.

That's what the LORD says. He calls Job "My servant" and says, "there is no one on earth like him." Then He adds that Job is blameless, upright, fears God and shuns evil. It's the same description the writer gave us in verse 1.
Verse 8 says the opposite. The LORD tells Satan, "there is no one on earth like him." He also calls Job "My servant." He's the one who brings Job up first.

explanations.answer: Job fears God only because God blesses him
explanations.explanation: Yes. Satan asks, "Does Job fear God for nothing?" Then he points to the hedge around Job and the blessing on the work of his hands. His claim is that Job's fear of God depends on what he gets. Satan is accusing him.

explanations.answer: Job deserves even more blessing from God
explanations.explanation: Satan isn't asking for more blessing for Job. He asks, "Does Job fear God for nothing?" and then wants everything Job has to be struck (Job 1:11). He's questioning why Job fears God.

explanations.answer: Job has been hiding his sins from God
explanations.explanation: Satan never says anything about hidden sins. He asks, "Does Job fear God for nothing?" Then he points to the hedge and the blessings. His charge is that Job's fear of God depends on what God gives him.
Satan says, "he will surely curse You to Your face." That's his bet. He says Job's loyalty will crack once his stuff is struck. The rest of this passage shows what Job actually does.
Praise is what Satan says Job won't do. He says that if everything Job has is struck, "he will surely curse You to Your face." He's betting against Job.
Obey isn't the word. Satan says that if Job's belongings are struck, "he will surely curse You to Your face." He thinks Job will turn on God, not just stop following orders.
That's right. The LORD says, "Everything he has is in your hands, but you must not lay a hand on the man himself." So Satan gets a limit. He can touch what Job owns, but not Job himself.
There is a limit, friend. The LORD tells Satan, "Everything he has is in your hands, but you must not lay a hand on the man himself." Satan doesn't get a free hand on Job himself.

The messenger says the Sabeans swooped down and took the oxen and donkeys away. It happens while the animals are plowing and grazing, so it's a normal workday for them. It's sudden, with no warning. That's a rough way to start the news.
No disease in this report. The messenger says the Sabeans swooped down and took the animals away (Job 1:15). People did this, and they carried the animals off.

explanations.answer: They ran off into the desert
explanations.explanation: The animals didn't wander off on their own. The messenger says the Sabeans swooped down and took them away (Job 1:15). The animals were taken.
Yes. Verse 16 says, "While he was still speaking, another messenger came." Job doesn't get a breath between reports. The news keeps coming.

It's true, friend. Verse 16 says, "While he was still speaking, another messenger came and reported." The first messenger doesn't even get to finish before the next one arrives. Job has no time to take it in.

explanations.answer: Fire fell from heaven and burned them
explanations.explanation: That's it. The second messenger says, "The fire of God fell from heaven. It burned and consumed the sheep and the servants." This one doesn't come from raiders. The sheep and the servants are both gone.

explanations.answer: Raiders drove them away to the north
explanations.explanation: Raiders show up in the first and third reports, not this one. The second messenger says, "The fire of God fell from heaven. It burned and consumed the sheep and the servants." The text doesn't mention the north.

explanations.answer: Wild animals scattered them in the night
explanations.explanation: No wild animals here, and no night either. The second messenger says, "The fire of God fell from heaven. It burned and consumed the sheep and the servants." That's the whole report.
Camels it is. The Chaldeans formed three bands, raided the camels and took them away. Job had 3,000 camels (Job 1:3). The third messenger arrives while the second is still speaking.
Goats aren't in this story. Job's list in verse 3 names sheep, camels, oxen and donkeys. The Chaldeans formed three bands and raided the camels.
No horses on Job's list, friend. Verse 3 names sheep, camels, oxen and donkeys. The raiders in this report took the camels.

The messenger says, "a mighty wind swept in from the desert and struck the four corners of the house." It collapsed on the young people, and they are dead. This is the heaviest news of the four. I think this one hurts the most.
No army this time. The messenger says, "a mighty wind swept in from the desert and struck the four corners of the house." This is the heaviest report of the four. Job's children were inside.

There's no flood in this report. The messenger says, "a mighty wind swept in from the desert and struck the four corners of the house." It's the heaviest news Job gets. His sons and daughters are gone.

explanations.answer: Falls to the ground and worships
explanations.explanation: Verse 20 says, "He fell to the ground and worshiped." He's torn his robe and shaved his head, so he's grieving, and he worships anyway. He doesn't cut off the grief or the worship. I think it's one of the most powerful moments in the Bible.
The text never says Job sends anyone after the raiders. After tearing his robe and shaving his head, "He fell to the ground and worshiped." His next move is toward God.

explanations.answer: Leaves the land of Uz for good
explanations.explanation: Job doesn't leave anywhere. The text says he stood up, tore his robe and shaved his head. Then "He fell to the ground and worshiped."
Job says, "Blessed be the name of the LORD." It comes right after, "The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away." He has just lost everything, and that's what he says. It's quiet and it's real.
Swearing isn't what Job does. After saying, "The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away," he says, "Blessed be the name of the LORD." He blesses the name.
It's the opposite. Job has lost nearly everything, and he says, "Blessed be the name of the LORD." He doesn't turn away from God's name. He blesses it.
Not at all. Verse 22 says, "In all this, Job did not sin or charge God with wrongdoing." Satan had said Job would curse God to His face (Job 1:11). That isn't what happens here.

Right, friend. Job 1:22 says, "In all this, Job did not sin or charge God with wrongdoing." He has lost his flocks, his servants and his children, and the text still says that. Satan said Job would curse God, and he didn't.
